title: My family
goal: Name family members and their jobs — and set up the thing that feels most foreign to English speakers: Pashto nouns have gender, and that gender spreads to adjectives and to "to be".
bekal: name father, mother, siblings, and children along with their jobs
tell masculine and feminine words apart by their endings
express possession with د and with زما، ستا، زمونږ

dialogs.title: خبرې اترې — د نجیب په کور کې
dialogs.intro: First evening in Kabul. Najib brings out his family photo album and sets it down on a floor cushion.

lines.text: دا زما پلار دی. هغه ښوونکی دی.

lines.literal: Afghan families big usually-are. of-me uncle, aunt and uncle all near live-they.

notes: Pashto nouns have gender, and that is the lesson of this unit. پلار (father) is masculine, مور (mother) feminine — so far, so logical. But کتاب (book) is also masculine and کورنۍ (family) is feminine, and there is nothing male or female about a book or a family. What decides it is **the shape of the word**, not its meaning.

Look at the pair ښوونکی and ډاکټره in the dialogue. Job titles have gender too: ښوونکی *ṣowunkay* is a male teacher, ښوونکې *ṣowunke* a female teacher; ډاکټر is masculine, ډاکټره feminine. If you use the wrong form, you will still be understood — but you will sound exactly like a foreigner.

Adjectives change too, and this is what people forget most often. Budi says ډېره ښکلې کورنۍ with the feminine form, because کورنۍ is feminine. For a masculine noun the form is ښکلی — for example ښکلی ښار, a beautiful city. One adjective, two faces.

The phrase نوم یې احمد دی deserves a closer look. The little word یې *ye* means "his/her", and it never stands at the start of a sentence — it always attaches after the first word. Small forms like this are covered fully in unit 17; for now, just recognize the pattern.

Asking "who is this?" also depends on gender. For a man it is دا څوک **دی**؟, for a woman دا څوک **ده**؟ — so before you ask, you already have to know whether the answer is a man or a woman. If you really don't know, use the masculine form; it counts as neutral.

Afghan families name relatives in more detail than English does. There is no single word for "uncle": تره is your father's brother, ماما is your mother's brother, and the two are never mixed up. The extra section of this unit lists them all.

grammars.title: Gender: how to guess it from the ending
body: The good news: Pashto marks gender at the end of the word, and the marks are fairly reliable. The first four rows of the table below cover most of the words you will meet in this course.

The less good news: the most common words are the ones that break the rules most often. مور (mother) and خور (sister) end in a consonant like masculine words, but both are feminine. Learn those two as exceptions and the rest will behave.

grammars.title: Possession: the owner comes first
body: English can put the owner first too: "Budi's book". Pashto always does, with the little word د in front of the owner: **د بودي کتاب**, literally "of Budi book".
Pronouns have short, fused forms, and those are what people use every day. Note that زما does not mean "I" but "my" — it can never be the subject of a sentence.

sections.title: The Afghan family, word by word

blocks.text: Your father's brother is not your mother's brother

This is where Pashto is far more precise than English. There is no general "uncle" or "aunt"; instead there are four different words that show which side of the family the link runs through. Getting them wrong does not make your sentence ungrammatical, but it instantly sounds like someone who doesn't know who belongs to whom.

head: Pashto
Say it
Exactly who
rows: Son of your تره — a cousin on your father's side.

blocks.title: ⚠️ One word with two faces: تربور
items: The word تربور means a cousin on your father's side, and in Afghanistan it carries a weight that the English word "cousin" does not. A paternal cousin is your closest relative and, at the same time, your most likely rival for an inheritance.
That is why there are Pashto proverbs about him, and a word تربورولي *tarbūrwalī* that means rivalry between cousins. English has no equivalent.
For a cousin on your mother's side, people say د ماما زوی *də māmā zoy*, literally "uncle's son" — there is no single word for it, and no weight attached.

blocks.title: A quick rule for adjectives
items: Adjectives ending in **ی** *-ay* change to **ې** *-e* before a feminine noun. For example ښکلی ښار becomes ښکلې کورنۍ.
Adjectives ending in a consonant add **ه** *-a*. For example بد becomes بده · ډېر becomes ډېره.
Some adjectives don't change at all, and the most common one is among them: **ښه** (good) is the same for masculine and feminine.
⚠️ Note that ډېر also means "very" and still agrees in gender: ډېره ښکلې کورنۍ, not ډېر ښکلې کورنۍ.

Choose the right form of the adjective for each noun.
Put the words in the right order.
